newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire talks to go ahead, Kinshasa under curfew.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks to go ahead, Kinshasa under curfew.

text.p: Zaire's embattled government announced an overnight curfew in the capital Kinshasa on Tuesday on the eve of fresh face-to-face talks between President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
With Kabila's rebels reportedly advancing on Kinshasa, Mobutu's emergency rule government imposed the curfew and said soldiers had orders to shoot anyone caught looting.
But mediators expressed optimism that South Africa's president Nelson Mandela could pull a last-minute deal out of the hat.
South African officials confirmed that Wednesday's meeting would go ahead as planned on the South African navy icebreaker SAS Outeniqua off Congo's port of Pointe Noire.

"I am optimistic that there will be a soft landing and a peaceful, inclusive transition, mainly because of South Africa's very strong and effective and skilful efforts in the past two days at mediating this crisis," U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson told reporters in New York.

A spokesman for Mandela, who hosted a first and inconclusive round of talks on the ship on May 4, told Reuters agreement had been reached on outlines of an accord to end the seven-month-old civil war.
"They have a skeleton of the main areas of agreement that are supposed to be ratified tomorrow," Joel Netshitenzhe said.
Zaire's Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba announced details of the curfew, the first of the war in the city.

In the city centre, Kinshasa's usually bustling streets emptied after the curfew took effect at 8 p.m. Families sat out on their balconies, speculating about what might happen. The curfew ends at 6 a.m.
Kabila insists that Mobutu must hand power to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.

He told a U.S. radio station on Monday a peaceful transfer of power depended on Mobutu, who seized power in Africa's third largest nation in 1965. "Mobutu has to go, to relinquish power to the alliance, that is on Wednesday," he said.
Reports reaching Kinshasa said the rebels had taken the key bridge over the River Kwango and Zaire's armed forces (FAZ) had pulled back to Mbankana about 150 km (100 miles) from the city.

Information Minister Kin-Kiey told Reuters he could make no immediate comment on the reports. On Monday, he told reporters there was fierce fighting in the region of Kenge, 60 km (40 miles) to the east of the bridge.
Kabila's son Joseph, a frontline commander, said on Monday the rebels were advancing on all fronts.
Mobutu, 66, is fighting cancer and a civil war.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, control three-quarters of Zaire.

Mobutu's son and spokesman Nzanga told Belgian RTL-TVI television on Monday his father was ready to make serious concessions, but he declined to go into detail. "Everything depends on the negotiations," he said.
The French Foreign Ministry, quoting "fully reliable sources", accused the rebels of killing refugees at Mbandaka, some 600 km (370 miles) north east of Kinshasa by river.
"France condemns these criminal acts and voices deep indignation. It appeals to all those who can join voices in immediately demanding that human lives be respected," it said.
The U.N. has airlifted home more than 22,000 Rwandan Hutus from rebel-held territory since April 27.
